scenario.name: Break Escape SAFETYNET: Mission 9 — Digital Archaeology VMs
scenario.author: Z. Cliffe Schreuders
scenario.description:
# Break Escape SAFETYNET Mission 9: Digital Archaeology
Virtual machines for the Break Escape SAFETYNET mission 9 narrative experience. The operative works in a records archive in Helena, Montana, and needs two old machines: the archive's catalogue server, and the last server of Tomb Beta, one of the Architect's closed workshops, racked in the tape room. The first machine holds the Insider Threat Initiative's ledger. The second holds the owner's credential, his memo on a flaw SAFETYNET catalogued and never reported, his unsent vendor notice, and the job that still mirrors the stolen database to Tomb Gamma.
The two machines are reached in different ways, and both are diegetic. The catalogue's restricted index opens only to the catalogue service account, whose login the game hands the operative on the reading-room duty-desk slip (authenticated access with a recovered credential). Tomb Beta's old lightweight web server is reached through an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw, landing on its web service account. After the foothold, a sudo misconfiguration on a common pager utility escalates each box to root.
## Included Systems
**catalogue_server** - Debian 12 desktop system - Hosts the archive's catalogue. The public catalogue is browsable, but the restricted index is reachable only by signing in as the catalogue service account. - Catalogue service account `catalogsvc` (password `Catalog!Helena2016`, the duty-desk slip) holds flag 1 in its home: the restricted catalogue index (Series R, R-114 to R-161, restricted cage bay 10) - Root's home holds flag 2, the Insider Threat Initiative's ledger (placements 23, candidates 47, WREN / H&L source file HL2015-0477), reached through a sudo rule on a common pager utility
**tomb_beta_server** - Debian 12 desktop system - Old lightweight web server on a random port, running under the web service account `nostromousr`. Reached through an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in the web server (no login required). - The web service account's home holds flag 3, a SAFETYNET staff credential issued to Dr Adrian Tesseract, which proves who owns the server. The same home holds the vulnerability-holdings record for the Albion control flaw (ref VH-2017-0312, Carrow Controls RM-4), Tesseract's memo to the Disposition Board, and his unsent vendor notice. - Root's home holds flag 4, a scheduled job that mirrors to Tomb Gamma, the publication hour, the head start for the cells, and the list of defences. Reached through a sudo rule on a common pager utility.
**attack_vm** - Kali Linux penetration testing platform - The field laptop and drop terminal in the reading room
## Flags
Flags 1 and 2 (the catalogue server) are submitted at the reading-room drop terminal. Flags 3 and 4 (Tomb Beta's server) are submitted at the drop link in the salvage cage, beside the machine they came from.
## Integration with Break Escape
These VMs are provisioned by the Break Escape game engine via SecGen integration. Players interact with these systems through the game's narrative and task system, with guided hints delivered via SAFETYNET field guides. The catalogue account name and password are the fixed strings the game prints on the reading-room duty-desk slip; they must match the catalogue account this VM builds. Tomb Beta is entered by exploitation, so its web service account needs no login credential.
## CyBOK Coverage
- Network mapping and service fingerprinting - Authenticated access using a recovered credential (catalogue server) - Unauthenticated remote code execution and its mitigation (Tomb Beta web server) - Access control and privilege escalation through sudo misconfiguration - Insider-threat investigation and document analysis - Cyber kill chain

CyBOK.keyword: Vulnerabilities and attacks on access control misconfigurations

MEMO To: Disposition Board From: Chief Strategist (Dr A. Tesseract) Date: 14 March 2017 Re: VH-2017-0312
We are holding a flaw in a Carrow controller because it may one day be useful to us. It will certainly one day be useful to someone else. Four hundred sites run this module. Their engineers cannot patch what nobody has told them about, and we cannot defend them from it, having chosen not to. I recommend notification to the vendor within thirty days. I have drafted the notice. I would rather send it than explain later why we didn't. A. Tesseract

DRAFT, NOT SENT Date: 14 March 2017 To: Product Security, Carrow Controls From: SAFETYNET Vulnerability Management (Dr A. Tesseract, Chief Strategist) Re: RM-4 remote-management module
We have found a flaw in the RM-4 module that lets an unauthenticated user on the management network issue control commands. A test case is attached for your engineers. We will keep this confidential for ninety days from the date of this letter, or until a fix ships, whichever is sooner, so that your customers have time to patch. We are glad to help with testing. With thanks, Dr Adrian Tesseract, Chief Strategist
